====================================================
Empirical Research Plan: 1985–1992 Cigarette Taxes & Birth Outcomes
====================================================

----------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered treatment adoption, implemented as a two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) event-study.

Why DID?  
• The “treatment” (state cigarette‐tax increases) varies across states and over time, providing the canonical DID setting.  
• Birth-certificate micro data contain rich covariates and very large N, letting us saturate fixed effects and flexibly model differential trends.  
• An event-study specification lets us (i) test for pre-treatment parallel trends, (ii) capture dynamic effects, and (iii) handle multiple tax changes per state.

Extension for mechanism: 2-Stage Least Squares (IV).  
1st stage: Tax → maternal smoking.  
2nd stage: Predicted smoking → birth outcome.  
The IV gives the causal effect of smoking conditional on exogeneity of taxes, while the reduced-form DID gives the policy effect of taxes themselves.

----------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: real cigarette-tax rate (cents per pack, CPI-adjusted).  
• Binary (for event-study): indicator = 1 for state-year (or state-month) in which the tax rate is strictly above its pre-change level (first year after each increase).

Control group  
• States in years before they increase taxes and states that never increase taxes during the window.  
• For the IV, untreated births (mothers in low-tax states/years) provide the first-stage counterfactual.

Treatment timing  
• Event date τs = month (or quarter) in which a new tax rate becomes effective in state s.  
• Event time k = t – τs in months (k = 0 is the first full month post change).

----------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends in absence of treatment.  
Plausibility: Pre-period dynamics in smoking behavior and birth outcomes tend to move smoothly; we can test this visually/inferentially with event-study leads.

A2. No simultaneous confounders that differentially affect treated states exactly when taxes change.  
Plausibility: Most maternal/child-health programs (e.g., Medicaid expansions) roll out on different calendars; still, we will explicitly control for them and run sensitivity checks.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) / no cross-state spillovers.  
Plausibility: Cigarette smuggling across borders is limited relative to pregnant women’s smoking demand and is likely orthogonal to birth outcomes in other states; we can probe border-county subsamples.

A4. Exogenous tax timing with respect to unobservable determinants of birth outcomes.  
Plausibility: Tax changes are largely revenue/health driven at legislatures, not by short-run shocks in pregnancy health; however, we test for pre-trends and add state-specific linear trends.

Additional for IV: Relevance (tax significantly reduces smoking) and exclusion (tax affects outcomes only through smoking). Both can be partially tested (F-stat>10; control for alternative channels such as income).

----------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigations
----------------------------------------------------
T1. Policy bundling (states raise cigarette taxes while passing other maternal-health legislation).  
  • Mitigation: Control for contemporaneous Medicaid eligibility thresholds, WIC coverage, clean-air laws, and state excise taxes on alcohol.  
  • Run robustness excluding years with large Medicaid eligibility expansions.

T2. Differential economic shocks (e.g., recessions hitting certain states).  
  • Mitigation: Include state-specific linear & quadratic time trends, state-month unemployment rate, and per-capita income.  
  • Placebo test on outcomes plausibly unrelated to smoking (e.g., infant sex ratio).

T3. Migration or cross-border cigarette purchases.  
  • Mitigation: Restrict to mothers residing >50 miles from a state border in robustness check.  
  • Use county-level average tax of nearest three states as alternative measure to account for smuggling.

----------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast load/manip
library(fixest)       # TWFE & IV
library(lubridate)    # date handling
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load & merge ----------------------------------------------------------
births <- fread("natality_1985_1992.csv")           # individual records
tax    <- fread("state_cigarette_taxes_1980_1995.csv")

# Ensure dates
tax[, eff_date := ymd(effective_date)]
births[, dob := ymd(date_of_birth)]

# Merge by state & date (use month granularity)
births[, year_month := floor_date(dob, "month")]
tax[, year_month := floor_date(eff_date, "month")]

setkey(births, state, year_month)
setkey(tax,    state, year_month)
births <- tax[births, roll=TRUE]   # carries forward last known tax

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
births[, real_tax := tax_cents / cpi_factor]  # CPI deflated
births[, post  := real_tax > shift(real_tax, 1, type="lag"), by = state]  # first-month change
# Continuous treatment
births[, treat_cont := real_tax]

# Event time (relative k in months)
births[, event_time := as.numeric(difftime(year_month, 
                             min(year_month[post==TRUE]), units="days"))/30, by=state]
# Cap leads/lags
births[(event_time < -24) , event_time := -24]
births[(event_time >  36) , event_time :=  36]

# Outcomes
births[, low_bw      := (birth_weight < 2500)]
births[, gest_weeks  := gestation_weeks]
births[, smoke       := (maternal_smoked == 1)]

# Covariates
covars <- c("maternal_age", "parity", "education_yrs", "married",
            "race_black", "race_hispanic", "prenatal_visits")

# 3. Main DID regression ---------------------------------------------------
did_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("birth_weight ~ treat_cont | state + year_month +", 
        paste(covars, collapse = " + "))
)

res_main <- feols(did_formula, data = births, weight = ~1)
summary(res_main)

# 4. Event-study -----------------------------------------------------------
event_formula <- birth_weight ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) | state + year_month + maternal_age + parity
res_event <- feols(event_formula, data = births[abs(event_time)<=36])
iplot(res_event)   # pre-trend check

# 5. IV for smoking mechanism ---------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- birth_weight ~ 1 | state + year_month | (smoke ~ treat_cont) + maternal_age + parity + education_yrs
res_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = births)
summary(res_iv)

# 6. Robustness: drop border counties -------------------------------------
res_rob <- feols(did_formula, data = births[border_county==0])
etable(list(Main = res_main, NoBorder = res_rob))
```

----------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------
Theory and previous public-health evidence imply:

• First stage: A 10-cent (≈10 %) real tax increase should reduce prenatal smoking by ~1–2 pp (elasticity ≈ −0.15 to −0.20 for pregnant smokers).

• Reduced form: Every 10-cent tax increase should raise average birth weight by ~3–6 grams and reduce low-birth-weight incidence by 0.1–0.2 pp.

• IV: One fewer cigarette per day during pregnancy should increase birth weight by 5–10 grams; complete cessation (~10 cigs/day) ≈ 50–100 grams.

Sign of effects: Tax ↑ → Smoking ↓ → Birth outcomes improve (higher weight, longer gestation).

----------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
----------------------------------------------------
C1. No pre-treatment trend differences……………… 1  
C2. No anticipation/behavioral timing shifts……… 0.8  
C3. No simultaneous confounding policies………… 0.7  
C4. No spillovers across units………………………… 0.8  
C5. Stable composition of sample over time……… 0.9  

Overall: 4.2 / 5 ≈ 84 % confidence in causal interpretation, subject to robustness and sensitivity analyses described above.

====================================================
